headline: US 10-year Treasury notes likely near a blow-off bottom; short positioning is historically extreme, and a fall in oil would catalyse a rally — expect yields to range between 4.00-4.25% on the low side and 5.00-5.50% on the high side
reasoning: Garner notes that US portfolios are very underweight Treasuries and short interest is close to historic extremes, meaning there is substantial latent buying power if shorts begin to cover or portfolios find a reason to deploy capital. A 25-year monthly chart of the 10-year Treasury note future shows price near a long-term trend line that has historically held. She links the Treasury outlook directly to oil: if oil is topping as she believes, Treasury notes should blow off their bottom and rally. She cannot rule out one more flush low that runs stops and forces liquidation, but sees that as a temporary risk rather than the primary scenario.
quote: The market's positioned in one side. Portfolios here in the US are very underweight treasuries, so there's a lot of buying power if the shorts start to cover and if portfolios find a reason to put money to work in treasuries, we could see a bottom. I think if oil is low off topping like I believe it is, we should see Treasury notes blow off bottom and start heading the other way. So look for interest rates on the ten year note to probably bottom out somewhere around between 5 and 5.5%. And on the upside, we might well on the downside in yields. If you're talking about yields in that price, roughly 4 to 4 to a quarter should be a pretty healthy ebb and flow.

headline: Oil likely topping; base case is a replay of 2022 pushing prices back into the 70s, with 40s possible thereafter and a tail risk of 125-150 if demand destruction fails to materialise
reasoning: Garner sees oil as already experiencing demand destruction while supply is surprisingly finding its way to market despite geopolitical headlines. Her base case is a decline similar to 2022 that takes prices into the 70s, with longer-term potential toward the 40s. She acknowledges an upside tail risk to $124-125 if bulls prevail, and above that level she sees a retest of the 2008 high around $150 as the only logical ceiling. An extreme downside scenario of $15 is also flagged based on cycle repetition seen in 2020, 2014 (fracking era) and other episodes, though she is not predicting it.
quote: I think a more likely scenario is we replay 2022 and that brings us down in the 70s. Then we can maybe start talking about those 40 numbers in this monthly chart. Points out an even crazier number, which is $15 a barrel. I'm not predicting 15, but the reality is, if the cycle repeats itself like it did in 2028 and a couple other occasions 2014 when fracking was invented, that is a possibility.

headline: Bearish crude oil base case: $105 resistance holds, targeting $72 then $41 over the next year, mirroring the 2022 post-Russia/Ukraine pattern
reasoning: Garner identifies $105 as a critical technical level where the daily uptrend line and weekly downtrend line converge, creating a decisive pivot. Her base case is that this level holds and crude oil replays the 2022 post-Ukraine-invasion pattern: a double top, a partial rally, and then a multi-year trend lower. The first major support on the way down is $72 (the 200-week moving average), but the weekly chart ultimately points to the low 40s over a one-year horizon. She acknowledges supply is finding its way to market despite headlines and sees demand destruction already in train.
quote: If it does play out like 20, 22, 105 should hold in October crude oil, and we should make our way down to, believe it or not, somewhere in the 40s. That's what the weekly chart suggests. Of course, there's going to be support around 72. That's the 200 week moving average. That's a daily chart trend line. So 72 is a big number. Obviously we have to get through that if we're going to talk about lower prices. So we'll start with 72. But keep 41 in mind. I'm not saying it gets there next month, but we're talking maybe a year or so from now. That is definitely a possibility.

headline: Bull risk scenario: break above $105 triggers rapid repricing to $121–$125, with $150 possible if control is lost entirely
reasoning: Garner flags a tail-risk bull scenario where $105 fails to hold as resistance. In that case she expects a swift move to $121–$125, a level derived from a 25-year monthly chart. If price then pushes above $125, she says all bets are off and the only next reference point is $150, last seen in 2008. She explicitly says this is not her base case, citing demand destruction and supply finding its way to market, but she includes it as a scenario investors must track.
quote: If I'm wrong and 105 doesn't hold suddenly, we probably get a very quick repricing. That brings us up to 12125. This is a monthly chart. This goes back 25 years, and you can get an idea of where I'm getting that 124125 ish area as a possibility. I am not I'm not in the camp that thinks that's going to happen. I think we're already seeing demand destruction. I think supply is miraculously finding its way to the market despite all the crazy headlines. So I'm not counting on that. But it is possible. Now, if I'm completely wrong and we start pushing above 125, all bets are off. Honestly, we're repricing and the only thing stopping it is $150 a barrel, which was seen in 2008 again.

headline: Fed 25bp hike criticised as merely symbolic; balance sheet reduction rather than rate rises is the right tool to fight inflation driven by excess liquidity
reasoning: Garner argues the Federal Reserve's rate hike is too small to matter and that a 50 or even 100bp move would have been needed to credibly signal seriousness. Her core view is that inflation is fundamentally a liquidity problem — too much money chasing too few assets — and the correct remedy is balance sheet reduction, not rate increases. She singles out commodity and energy prices as the biggest inflation drivers, suggesting monetary policy alone cannot solve the problem.
quote: I'm not a fan of it. I feel like, you know, obviously we have a problem here in the United States with inflation. In fact, it's a global problem. Raising interest rates might be one tool that they could use to help with inflation, but the biggest tool they have is the fed balance sheet. In my opinion, we have way too much money sloshing around the system. Too much money chasing too few assets causes inflation. I think that's really what it is. I wish the fed would have left rates where they were and pulled back balance sheet funds. In other words, pull liquidity from the marketplace. That said, they they did what they did. But the problem is they didn't do enough. If they were going to raise rates, they probably should have gotten 50 basis points or maybe even 100. Just really, you know, kind of shocked the market.
